## Introduction

How well does a network keep functioning as its nodes disappear? Albert,
Jeong & Barabasi (2000) <doi:10.1038/35019019> showed that many real
networks respond very differently to two kinds of node loss: **random
failure**, where nodes disappear independently of any property of the
network, and **targeted attack**, where the most "important" nodes (by
degree, betweenness, or another centrality) are removed first. Some
networks barely notice random failure but collapse quickly under a
targeted attack on their hubs.

netRobust simulates both scenarios on any `igraph` object -- directed or
undirected, weighted or not -- tracks a set of robustness indicators
(giant component size, average path length, connectivity, and others) as
nodes are removed, and provides a Monte Carlo framework for asking
whether an observed curve is *statistically* more damaging than chance
alone would produce. This vignette walks through that full workflow, end
to end, on a small, well-known example network.

## Setup

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(netRobust)
library(igraph)
```

One dependency is optional and only changes *how* the Monte Carlo
simulations run, never their results:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession)   # parallelise replicates across cores
```

Sequential replicates already show a console progress indicator (a
spinner and percentage) with no setup needed -- it's skipped when
running in parallel, since a `future.apply` worker has no access to the
parent session's console.

## Example network: Zachary's Karate Club

We'll use Zachary's Karate Club, one of the most familiar example
networks in network science: 34 members of a university karate club and
the 78 friendships between them, recorded before the club famously split
in two.

```{r}
g <- make_graph("Zachary")
g
```

```{r}
plot(g, vertex.label = NA, vertex.size = 8, vertex.color = "steelblue",
     edge.color = "grey70", main = "Zachary's Karate Club")
```

It's undirected and unweighted, which keeps most of the workflow below
free of extra arguments. Section
["A note on direction and weights"](#a-note-on-direction-and-weights)
covers what changes for directed/weighted networks.

## Removal orders

Every scenario in netRobust starts from a **removal order**: which
vertex goes first, second, and so on. `random_failures()` generates a
uniformly random order; `attack_by_degree()` removes the highest-degree
("hub") vertices first, the classic attack criterion from Albert et al.
(2000).

```{r}
set.seed(1)
r <- random_failures(g)
d <- attack_by_degree(g)
head(d)
```

Both return the same shape: a named integer vector, first element =
first vertex removed. Four more targeted-attack criteria exist --
`attack_by_betweenness()`, `attack_by_closeness()`,
`attack_by_eigenvector()`, and `attack_by_pagerank()` -- with the same
`function(g) -> removal order` contract. They come back in
["Statistical comparison across attack strategies"](#statistical-comparison-across-attack-strategies).

## A note on direction and weights

On a directed graph, "degree" is ambiguous: a vertex can have many
incoming connections and few outgoing ones, or vice versa. Every
`attack_by_*()` function exposes `mode = c("all", "out", "in")` (ignored
on undirected graphs, like the Karate Club above) to control which one
drives the attack. To see why this matters, take a tiny directed toy
graph with one "out-hub" and one "in-hub":

```{r}
toy <- graph_from_literal(A -+ B, A -+ C, A -+ D, B -+ D, C -+ D, E -+ D)
```

```{r}
plot(toy, edge.arrow.size = 0.6, vertex.color = "steelblue",
     main = "A has the highest out-degree, D the highest in-degree")
```

```{r}
attack_by_degree(toy, mode = "out")   # A goes first: highest out-degree
attack_by_degree(toy, mode = "in")    # D goes first: highest in-degree
```

Same graph, same criterion (degree), opposite first casualty -- purely
because of which direction "degree" was counted in. `robustness()` and
the `attack_by_*()` functions default to `directed = NULL`, which
auto-detects from `is_directed(g)`; pass `directed =` explicitly only to
override that.

The betweenness/closeness/eigenvector/PageRank attacks take a parallel
`weights_as = c("distance", "strength")` argument for *weighted*
networks, telling netRobust how to interpret an edge weight: as a
**distance** (bigger weight = farther apart, used as-is) or as a
**strength** (bigger weight = closer/stronger tie, inverted before
being used as a distance). Both `toy` and the Karate Club above have no
weights, so this has no effect on the examples in this vignette --
this argument only matters once `E(g)$weight` is set.

## Robustness curves

`robustness()` takes a removal order and returns one row per removal
step, with one column per indicator. `keep =` picks a subset of the
built-in indicators (see `?robustness` for the full default set, and how
to add your own via `indicators =`):

```{r}
failure <- robustness(g, ids = r, keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))
attack  <- robustness(g, ids = d, keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))
head(attack)
```

`GC` (giant component size) already tells a story: removing hub nodes
by degree shrinks it far faster than removing the same number of random
nodes. But `failure` here is a single random draw -- one arbitrary
sample out of the enormous space of possible removal orders. The next
section builds the full distribution instead of relying on one sample.

## Building a null model

`robustness_null_removal()` repeats `random_failures()` +
`robustness()` many times on the *same* network, producing the
empirical distribution of every indicator at every removal step --
i.e., what random failure alone typically looks like, and how much it
varies. `summarise_null()` collapses that into a mean/median and a 95%
quantile envelope, ready for plotting.

```{r}
null_dist <- robustness_null_removal(g, n_reps = 200, seed = 123,
                                      keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))
null_env  <- summarise_null(null_dist)
head(null_env)
```

The `...` in `robustness_null_removal(g, ..., keep = c(...))` must match
whatever settings were used for the observed curve it will be compared
against (here, `attack`) -- same indicators, same `directed =`/weights
treatment -- for the comparison to be valid.

## Plotting

A single random draw isn't a meaningful stand-in for "the failure
scenario" once hundreds of replicates of it already exist. So instead of
plotting one arbitrary `failure` curve, we plot the null distribution's
**median** curve -- reshaping `summarise_null()`'s long-format output
back into the wide, per-indicator shape `robustness()` produces:

```{r}
failure_median <- tidyr::pivot_wider(null_env, id_cols = N,
                                      names_from = Index, values_from = median)
```

```{r, warning = FALSE}
fig <- plot_robustness(failure = failure_median, attack = attack,
                        null_envelope = null_env)
fig
```

When `null_envelope` is supplied, `plot_robustness()` automatically
labels that curve "Failures (median)" and adds a caption explaining the
shaded band -- no need to track that distinction by hand.

## Statistical comparison across attack strategies

Two complementary questions remain: *at which removal step* does the
attack become significantly worse than random failure, and *overall*,
how much worse is it -- and how does that compare across all five attack
criteria?

`compare_to_null()` answers the first, step by step, with an empirical
p-value per indicator:

```{r}
sig <- compare_to_null(attack, null_dist)
head(sig[order(sig$p_value), ])
```

For the second, `robustness_index()` reduces a whole curve to one
number -- the R-index of Schneider et al. (2011): the mean of an
indicator's curve, normalised to its intact-network value (`1` = no
degradation at all, near `0` = the network collapses almost
immediately). `compare_robustness()` applies it across several
deterministic attack curves at once; `robustness_index_null()` is its
counterpart for a null distribution's many replicates (averaging the
R-index *per replicate*, not the R-index of an already-averaged curve --
see `?robustness_index_null` for why that distinction matters).

```{r}
b <- attack_by_betweenness(g)
c <- attack_by_closeness(g)
e <- attack_by_eigenvector(g)
p <- attack_by_pagerank(g)

attack_b <- robustness(g, ids = b, keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))
attack_c <- robustness(g, ids = c, keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))
attack_e <- robustness(g, ids = e, keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))
attack_p <- robustness(g, ids = p, keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))

r_index_attacks <- compare_robustness(scenario_list = list(
  Degree = attack, Betweenness = attack_b, Closeness = attack_c,
  Eigenvector = attack_e, PageRank = attack_p
), index = "GC")

r_index_failures <- data.frame(Scenario = "Failures",
                                R_index = robustness_index_null(null_dist, index = "GC"))

rbind(r_index_failures, r_index_attacks)
```

Every targeted attack scores well below random failure on this network
-- the Karate Club, like most real networks with a handful of highly
connected hubs, is far more vulnerable to targeted attacks than to
random ones.

## Structural null model

`robustness_null_removal()` asks: *given this exact network, does this
attack strategy do more damage than chance?* A different question is:
*is this network's structure itself unusually vulnerable to this attack
strategy, compared to other networks the same size with the same degree
sequence?* `robustness_null_structural()` answers that one instead, by
rewiring the network (preserving each vertex's degree) rather than
randomising the removal order:

```{r}
struct_null <- robustness_null_structural(g, attack_fn = attack_by_degree,
                                           n_reps = 200, seed = 123,
                                           keep = c("GC", "APL", "Connectivity"))
robustness_index_null(struct_null, index = "GC")
```

This is a **pure topological** null model: edge weights, if any, are
dropped before rewiring, since there's no principled way to carry them
over onto a randomised topology. Pass a weight-agnostic `attack_fn` (like
`attack_by_degree` above) when using it.

## Where to go next

Every function used here has a `?` help page with the full set of
arguments and further detail -- start with `?robustness`,
`?robustness_null_removal`, and `?robustness_null_structural` -- or
browse everything at once with `help(package = "netRobust")`.
